newsitem.title: VIRGIN ISLANDS: Clinton launches strategy to stop teen pregnancies.
newsitem.headline: Clinton launches strategy to stop teen pregnancies.

text.p: President Bill Clinton said on Saturday he was launching a national strategy to combat teen pregnancies, even as he hailed a decline in the teen birth rate in some states.

"The teen pregnancy rate is still intolerably high in America. Too many children are still having children. So we must do more," Clinton said in his weekly radio address. Clinton taped the address while on vacation on St. Thomas in the U.S. Virgin Islands.

Clinton said a key feature of his plan would be to encourage adolescents to abstain from sex. The White House said his aim was to send a strong message to all teenagers that postponing sexual activity, staying in school and preparing for work should be top goals.

Clinton called on Americans to support his strategy by helping get across to young people the idea that, "It's wrong to be pregnant or father a child unless you are married and ready to take on the responsibilities of parenthood."
At the same time, Clinton cited new state-by-state teen birth data that showed 37 states had a sustained decline in their teen birth rates between 1991 and 1994.

Twenty-one states had declines of between 5 and 10 percent, and 10 states had declines of more than 10 percent over this period. Overall the national birth rate for teens between the ages of 15 and 19 declined for the fourth year in a row, decreasing by 8 percent between 1991 and 1995, the White House said.

"We've made some significant progress in the effort against teen pregnancy in the last few years," Clinton said. "With the new steps I'm announcing today, we'll continue our fight against children having children."
While Clinton focused on progress in lowering the number of teen pregnancies, Republicans in their weekly radio response targeted a sharp increase in teen drug use.

"After 11 years of declining marijuana use among children ages 12 to 17, its use has doubled since 1992," said Sen. Paul Coverdell, R-Ga. "Among eighth graders, use of marijuana has tripled since 1991."

He suggested greater supervision by parents and less violence and glorification of drug use in movies, music and other entertainment. Coverdell also suggested giving parents the right to choose the schools their children attend.
In discussing out-of wedlock births to teenage mothers, Clinton was dealing with an issue that has been blamed for burdening the U.S. welfare system and contributing to crime.
His new strategy was aimed at carrying out some of the requirements of the new welfare law passed by the Republican-led Congress and signed by Clinton last August.

One directive under the law requires that at least 25 percent of American communities have teen pregnancy prevention programmes. It also provides $50 million a year in new funding for tate abstinence education activities.
Some $7.5 million will go toward pioneering programmes like one at Emory University in Atlanta where young people teach their peers about abstinence and responsibility.
